title: The Divergence Theorem and Classical Stokes

items.title: Divergence and curl of a $C^1$ vector field
Divergence and curl are linear and satisfy the scalar product rules
items.strategy: Both operators are finite sums of first partial derivatives of the components, so linearity is the sum and scalar rules for partial derivatives applied coordinate by coordinate. For a $C^1$ scalar $f$ expand $\partial_j(fF_i)=(\partial_jf)F_i+f\partial_jF_i$ and collect: the first group is $\langle\nabla f,F\rangle$ in the divergence and $\nabla f\times F$ in the curl, matching the coordinate formula of the cross product entry by entry, and the second group is $f$ times the operator. Check each of the three curl coordinates separately against the published coordinate definition rather than asserting the pattern.

items.title: The divergence and curl of a cross product
items.strategy: Write out the three coordinates of $F\times G$ from the published coordinate formula and differentiate each with the product rule. Collecting the six terms of $\operatorname{div}(F\times G)$ gives $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle$. For the curl, collect the twelve terms into $(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F$, where $DF\,G$ is the derivative matrix applied to $G$, identified with the vector of directional derivatives by the published total-derivative theorem. Do one coordinate in full and obtain the other two by the same computation, not by a symmetry claim.

items.title: A $C^1$ field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ is closed exactly when its curl vanishes
items.strategy: Closedness is the system of three independent equations $\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j$ for $i\ne j$ in three coordinates, and the three coordinates of the curl are exactly the three differences $\partial_jF_i-\partial_iF_j$ for those index pairs. Match the pairs explicitly, noting that the diagonal equations $i=j$ are trivial and that the pair $(i,j)$ and the pair $(j,i)$ give the same equation, so the three curl coordinates exhaust the system. Both directions are the same matching read in the two directions.

items.title: The curl of the gradient of a $C^2$ function vanishes
items.strategy: For $C^2$ $\phi$ the field $\nabla\phi$ is $C^1$, so its curl is defined. Each coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi$ is a difference $\partial_j\partial_i\phi-\partial_i\partial_j\phi$ of mixed second partials, which vanishes by the published Clairaut-Schwarz theorem. Do all three coordinates. Record that $C^2$ is used twice: once so that the gradient is $C^1$ and once as the hypothesis of Clairaut-Schwarz.

items.title: The divergence of the curl of a $C^2$ field vanishes
items.strategy: For $C^2$ $F$ the field $\operatorname{curl}F$ is $C^1$, so its divergence is defined. Expanding gives six second partials in three cancelling pairs, each pair equal by the published Clairaut-Schwarz theorem. Write the six terms out rather than appealing to a pattern, and record where each $C^2$ hypothesis is used.

items.title: The Laplacian of a $C^2$ function and of a $C^2$ vector field
The curl of a curl is the gradient of the divergence minus the Laplacian
items.strategy: Expand one coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$ from the coordinate definition, add and subtract the missing pure second derivative in that coordinate, and use Clairaut-Schwarz to exchange the mixed partials into $\partial$ of the divergence. The remainder is the componentwise Laplacian. Carry out each of the three coordinates; the identity needs $F$ to be $C^2$ for the curl of the curl to be defined and for the exchange to be licensed.

items.title: A $C^1$ field with vanishing curl on a star-shaped open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ is conservative
items.strategy: The curl-free hypothesis is closedness by the preceding corollary, and the published star-shaped equivalence turns closedness into exactness, conservativity, path independence and the vanishing of every closed-loop integral. State all five equivalent conclusions rather than only the potential, and record that the converse direction is the curl of a gradient vanishing, which needs the potential to be $C^2$ as the published equivalence supplies.

items.title: Vector potentials of a $C^1$ field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$
A divergence-free $C^1$ field on a star-shaped open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ has a vector potential
items.strategy: Let $U$ be star-shaped about $a$ and set $A(x)=\int_0^1 t\,B(a+t(x-a))\times(x-a)\,dt$, the exact analogue of the published star-shaped potential formula. Differentiating under the integral sign on a compact rectangle is licensed because the integrand and its parameter derivatives are continuous. Apply the cross-product curl identity with the first factor $x\mapsto B(a+t(x-a))$ and the second factor $x\mapsto x-a$: the second has divergence $3$ and derivative the identity, and the first has divergence $t(\operatorname{div}B)(a+t(x-a))=0$, leaving $2B(z_t)+t\,DB(z_t)(x-a)$. Multiplying by $t$ makes the integrand $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t^2B(z_t)\bigr)$, so Newton-Leibniz in $t$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A=B(x)$ with the $t=0$ endpoint contributing zero. Check that $A$ has continuous first partials, so it is $C^1$ and its curl is defined.

items.title: The curl measures the antisymmetric part of the total derivative
items.strategy: For a $C^1$ field $F$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ and vectors $u,v$, expand $\langle DF(p)u,v\rangle-\langle DF(p)v,u\rangle$ in coordinates as $\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jF_i-\partial_iF_j)u_jv_i$. Group the three index pairs, identify each coefficient with a coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}F(p)$, and recognise the resulting bilinear expression as $\langle\operatorname{curl}F(p),u\times v\rangle$ using the coordinate formula for the cross product. Verify the identity on the three pairs of standard basis vectors as a check on signs, and note that the diagonal terms $i=j$ contribute nothing.

items.title: A $C^1$ map sends a compact set of content zero to a set of content zero
items.strategy: Let $\psi$ be $C^1$ on an open $W\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and let $A\subseteq W$ be compact of content zero. Cover $A$ by finitely many closed cubes contained in $W$. On one such cube $Q$ the derivative norm is bounded, and applying the published mean value inequality to $t\mapsto\psi(x+t(y-x))$ along the segment joining two points of the convex set $Q$ makes $\psi$ Lipschitz on $Q$. Compose with the coordinatewise clamping retraction of $\mathbb R^m$ onto $Q$, which is $1$-Lipschitz because $r\mapsto\min\{\max\{r,\alpha\},\beta\}$ is, to obtain a Lipschitz map defined on all of $\mathbb R^m$ agreeing with $\psi$ on $Q$. The published Lipschitz-image theorem sends the null set $A\cap Q$ to a null set; a finite union of null sets is null; and the image is compact, so compactness turns null back into content zero. Treat the empty set separately.

items.title: Additivity of the integral over finitely many Jordan pieces that fill a Jordan set up to content zero
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a bounded Jordan set, let $A_1,\dots,A_N$ with $N\ge1$ be Jordan subsets of $A$ whose pairwise intersections have content zero and with $\operatorname{cont}(A\setminus\bigcup_iA_i)=0$, and let $f$ be bounded on $A$ and integrable on $A$ and on every $A_i$. Work with the zero extensions to one bounding rectangle. The difference between the sum of the extensions and the extension from $A$ is bounded by $(N+1)\sup|f|$ and vanishes off the union of the pairwise intersections with the residual set, a finite union of content-zero sets and therefore itself Jordan of content zero. Linearity and the absolute-value estimate then force that difference to integrate to zero. The case $N=1$ is the residual estimate alone, and the empty index set is excluded by $N\ge1$.

items.title: Change of variables for a $C^1$ map injective and regular only on the interior of a compact Jordan set
items.strategy: Let $\psi$ be $C^1$ on an open $W\supseteq D$ with $D$ compact Jordan, injective on $D^{\circ}$ and with nonvanishing Jacobian determinant there, and put $V=\psi[D^{\circ}]$. The inverse function theorem makes $\psi$ restricted to $D^{\circ}$ a diffeomorphism onto the open set $V$. Since $\partial(D^{\circ})\subseteq\partial D$ and $\psi[\partial D]$ has content zero by the preceding lemma, both $D^{\circ}$ and $V$ are bounded open Jordan sets. Take a compact grid exhaustion $K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\cdots$ of $D^{\circ}$ with vanishing content remainder and apply the published compact change-of-variables theorem on each $K_j$ with the open set $D^{\circ}$ as ambient domain. The parameter side converges because the integrand is bounded on the compact $D$ and $\operatorname{cont}(D\setminus K_j)\to0$. For the image side, apply the same exhaustion lemma to $V$ itself: each of its compact pieces lies in some $\psi[K_j]$, so $\operatorname{cont}(V\setminus\psi[K_j])\to0$ and the bounded integrand contributes vanishingly little. Handle an empty interior and a constant sign of the determinant explicitly.

items.title: A cyclic permutation of the coordinates of $\mathbb R^3$ preserves Jordan measurability and integrals
items.strategy: A cyclic permutation of coordinates is a linear bijection of $\mathbb R^3$ whose matrix has determinant $1$, so it is $C^1$ with everywhere invertible derivative and unit absolute Jacobian. The published compact change-of-variables theorem then gives measurability of the image and equality of the integrals with no scale factor. State the transport in the direction that will be used, namely that the integral of $H$ over $E$ equals the integral of $H$ composed with the inverse permutation over the permuted set, and record the determinant computation explicitly rather than asserting that a permutation matrix has determinant $1$.

items.title: Simple solid regions in a coordinate direction and their cyclic coordinate projection
Each coordinate of the oriented area vector is the Jacobian determinant of the matching cyclic projection
items.strategy: For a $C^1$ map $\varphi$ of two variables into $\mathbb R^3$ write out $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v$ from the published coordinate formula. Its $x$ coordinate is the two-by-two determinant of the derivative of $(\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its $y$ coordinate that of $(\varphi_z,\varphi_x)$, and its $z$ coordinate that of $(\varphi_x,\varphi_y)$. The cyclic order of the retained coordinates is what makes all three read the same way, and it is exactly the order fixed by the projection in the preceding definition; verify each of the three separately, since the middle one is the case where the naive increasing order gives the opposite sign.

items.title: The outward unit normal at a boundary point of a compact solid
Boundary presentations adapted to a simple solid region in a coordinate direction
The flux of a single-component field through a graph face is a base integral of its trace
items.strategy: Let $(D_j,\varphi_j)$ be a regular patch whose image lies in the graph of a continuous $\gamma$ over a compact Jordan base $D$ in direction $k$, and put $\psi=\pi_k\circ\varphi_j$. Injectivity of $\psi$ on $D_j^{\circ}$ is forced, not assumed: two interior parameter points with the same projection have the same image, because both images lie on the graph of a function, and the patch definition forbids that. By the projected-Jacobian lemma the hypothesis on the sign of the $k$ coordinate of the oriented area vector is exactly a sign hypothesis on $\det D\psi$ in the interior, so the degenerate-boundary change-of-variables lemma applies with $f(w)=R(w,\gamma(w))$ written in the projected coordinates. Replacing $|\det D\psi|$ by $\pm\det D\psi$ changes the integrand only on the content-zero parameter boundary. Both sign cases are stated; the vanishing of the integrand where the determinant vanishes on the boundary is what makes the two agree.

items.title: The single-direction flux identity on a simple solid region
items.strategy: Split the flux over the presentation into its three sublists. A lateral patch contributes zero because its integrand is the product of a continuous function with the $k$ coordinate of the oriented area vector, which vanishes on the parameter interior and hence, by continuity and the density of the interior in a compact Jordan parameter region, everywhere. The upper patches contribute the base integral of $R$ composed with the upper graph and the lower patches its negative, by the graph-face lemma summed with the almost-partition additivity lemma over the disjoint projected images. On the volume side, transport by the cyclic permutation lemma into the coordinate order the published solid-between-graphs Fubini formula uses, then evaluate the inner integral by the second fundamental theorem of calculus, whose integrand is continuous. Where the two graphs agree the inner integral and the increment are both zero, so that degenerate slice needs its own line.

items.title: At interior base points, the graph faces of an adapted presentation induce the outward unit normal
items.strategy: Fix an upper patch and an interior parameter point whose projection lies in the interior of the base. The projected map has invertible derivative there, so the inverse function theorem exhibits the graph function as the composite of the third patch component with the local inverse; hence the graph function is $C^1$ near that projected point and its graph has the patch's tangent plane. The induced normal is therefore a positive multiple of $(-\partial\gamma,1)$ in the projected coordinates, and moving off the surface along it changes the $k$ coordinate faster than the graph function can follow, so the forward points leave the solid. The backward points stay inside because the two graphs are strictly separated on the base interior. The lower case is the same argument with the signs reversed; the hypothesis that the projection lands in the base interior is used and is not removable.

items.title: Elementary solid regions: one boundary presentation adapted in all three coordinate directions
Every patch of an elementary solid region's presentation is a graph face in some direction, and at interior base points its normal is outward
items.strategy: A patch that is lateral for all three directions would have an induced unit normal orthogonal to each of the three standard basis vectors, hence zero, which contradicts its being a unit vector. So each patch is an upper or a lower face in at least one direction, and the preceding proposition gives outwardness at the parameter-interior points whose projection lands in that direction's base interior. State the conclusion with that qualification rather than for every boundary point; the excluded points are exactly the seams and edges.

items.title: The divergence theorem on an elementary solid region
items.strategy: Write $F$ as the sum of its three single-component fields. The same presentation is adapted in each direction, so the coordinate flux identity applies three times to the same boundary integral, and its three right-hand sides are the integrals of the three summands of the divergence. Add them with linearity of the flux sum and of the volume integral. Record that the sum of the three identities is where the requirement of one common presentation is used, and that the outward reading of the normal is the preceding corollary.

items.title: Finite gluings of elementary solid regions and their outward boundary presentation
Internal faces cancel and volume integrals add when elementary solid regions are glued
items.strategy: For the flux clause, the supplied gluing data pairs every internal patch with a patch of another piece that is an orientation-reversing reparametrization of it. The published flux reparametrization theorem negates the flux across such a pair, so each pair contributes zero and the surviving patches are the outer presentation; this is a rearrangement of a finite sum of reals and needs no connectedness. For the volume clause, each piece is a solid between continuous graphs and therefore compact and Jordan measurable, so its boundary has content zero and the pieces have pairwise disjoint interiors; the almost-partition additivity lemma then adds the piece integrals to the integral over the union, with the continuous integrand bounded on the compact union. The single-piece case has no internal pair and is included.

items.title: The divergence theorem for finite gluings of elementary solid regions
items.strategy: Apply the elementary-solid divergence theorem to each piece and sum. Both clauses of the cancellation lemma convert the two sums into the boundary flux over the outer presentation and the volume integral over the union. The field must be $C^1$ on an open set containing the whole union, since the piecewise identities are applied with that same field. State that the supplied decomposition and gluing data are part of the hypothesis and that nothing is asserted for a solid presented without them.

items.title: Vector forms: the boundary integrals of $fn$ and of $n\times F$
items.strategy: For a fixed vector $c$ apply the divergence theorem to $fc$: the product rule makes its divergence $\langle\nabla f,c\rangle$ because $c$ is constant, and the boundary integrand is $f\langle c,n\rangle$. Since the resulting identity holds for every $c$, taking $c$ over the standard basis identifies the two vector integrals coordinate by coordinate. For the second clause apply the theorem to $F\times c$, whose divergence is $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,c\rangle$ by the cross-product identity with a constant second factor, and rewrite $\langle F\times c,n\rangle$ as $\langle c,n\times F\rangle$ with the scalar triple product. Both clauses need the vector integrals to be defined coordinatewise, which is what the basis argument supplies.

items.title: The volume of a glued elementary solid is a third of the outward flux of the position field
items.strategy: The position field $p\mapsto p$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with divergence the constant $3$, so the divergence theorem turns its outward boundary flux into three times the integral of $1$ over the solid, which is the solid's Jordan content by the published indicator characterisation. Record the three one-coordinate variants obtained from the fields $xe_x$, $ye_y$ and $ze_z$, each with divergence $1$, and note that the solid is Jordan measurable because each glued piece is.

items.title: A field with vanishing divergence has zero outward flux through the boundary of a glued elementary solid
items.strategy: The divergence theorem turns the boundary flux into the volume integral of the zero function. State the hypothesis as it is used: the field is $C^1$ and divergence-free on an open set containing the whole solid, not merely on the boundary surface, and the companion page records what fails when only the second holds.

items.title: The flux of a curl through the boundary of a glued elementary solid vanishes
items.strategy: State the hypothesis as $F$ of class $C^2$ on an open set containing the solid, and say where $C^2$ is used: $\operatorname{curl}F$ is built from the first partial derivatives of the components of $F$, so it is $C^1$ exactly when $F$ is $C^2$, and $C^1$ is what the divergence-free corollary requires of the field it is applied to. Then $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0$ by the degree-two identity, so $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ divergence-free field on that open set and the preceding corollary gives zero outward flux through the boundary presentation. Do not weaken the hypothesis to $C^1$: with $F$ only $C^1$ the divergence of $\operatorname{curl}F$ need not be defined at all, so neither the identity nor the divergence theorem applies to it.

items.title: The divergence at a point is the limit of outward flux per unit volume
items.strategy: For a sequence of glued elementary solids containing $p$, of positive volume and with diameters tending to zero, the divergence theorem writes the flux as the volume integral of the divergence. Subtract the constant $\operatorname{div}F(p)$ inside the integral and estimate by the supremum of $|\operatorname{div}F-\operatorname{div}F(p)|$ over the solid times its volume; continuity of the divergence at $p$ and the vanishing diameters send that supremum to zero. No lower bound on the volume relative to the diameter is needed because the volume cancels. Record that positive volume is required only so the quotient is defined.

items.title: Green's first identity on a glued elementary solid region
items.strategy:
Apply the divergence theorem to the field $u
abla v$, which is $C^1$ when $u$ is $C^1$ and $v$ is $C^2$. The scalar product rule makes its divergence $\langle
abla u,
abla vangle+u\Delta v$, and its boundary integrand is $u$ times the normal derivative $\langle
abla v,nangle$. State the regularity of $u$ and $v$ exactly as used, and note that no symmetry between them is claimed at this stage.

items.title: Green's second identity on a glued elementary solid region
items.strategy: Write the first identity twice, once as it stands and once with $u$ and $v$ interchanged, which needs both functions to be $C^2$. Subtract: the inner-product terms are equal and cancel, leaving the difference of the two Laplacian terms on the left and the difference of the two normal-derivative terms on the right. Record the symmetry hypothesis explicitly, since it is stronger than the first identity's.

items.title: The induced boundary chain and circulation of a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region
A vector line integral along an image arc is the parameter line integral of the pulled-back field
items.strategy: Let $\sigma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ arc in the parameter region and $\varphi$ a $C^1$ map on a neighbourhood of it. On each smooth piece the chain rule gives $(\varphi\circ\sigma)'=\varphi_u\sigma_1'+\varphi_v\sigma_2'$, so the integrand $\langle F(\varphi\circ\sigma),(\varphi\circ\sigma)'\rangle$ equals $P^{*}\sigma_1'+Q^{*}\sigma_2'$ with $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$. Summing over the pieces of an admissible partition gives the parameter line integral. Check that $\varphi\circ\sigma$ is piecewise $C^1$ with the composed derivative as its continuous extension on each piece, and treat a degenerate constant piece, whose contribution is zero on both sides.

items.title: The curl flux integrand of a $C^2$ patch is a two-dimensional curl of the pulled-back field
items.strategy: With $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$, differentiate each by the product rule. The two terms carrying second derivatives of $\varphi$ are $\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_{uv}\rangle$ and $\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_{vu}\rangle$; they cancel in $\partial_uQ^{*}-\partial_vP^{*}$ by Clairaut-Schwarz applied to each component of $\varphi$, and this is the only place $C^2$ is used. The chain rule turns the remaining terms into $\langle DF(\varphi)\varphi_u,\varphi_v\rangle-\langle DF(\varphi)\varphi_v,\varphi_u\rangle$, which the antisymmetric-part lemma identifies with $\langle\operatorname{curl}F(\varphi),\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rangle$. Note that no regularity of the patch is used, so the identity holds at parameter points where the cross product vanishes.

items.title: The classical Stokes theorem for a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region
items.strategy: The pulled-back functions $P^{*}$ and $Q^{*}$ are $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of the parameter region because $\varphi$ is $C^2$ and $F$ is $C^1$ there. Green's theorem on that finite elementary Green region therefore equates the boundary-chain integral of $P^{*}\,du+Q^{*}\,dv$ with the region integral of $\partial_uQ^{*}-\partial_vP^{*}$. The pullback lemma identifies the left side arc by arc with the circulation around the induced boundary chain, and the integrand lemma identifies the right side with the flux of the curl in the orientation induced by $\varphi$. Shrink the neighbourhood so that its image lies in the domain of $F$, which compactness allows. Record that no regularity of the patch is needed for the identity itself, only for reading the right side as a flux.

items.title: A curl-free field has zero circulation around the induced boundary chain of a $C^2$ patch
items.strategy: Stokes' theorem writes the circulation as the flux of the curl, which is the integral of the zero function. Say exactly which set the curl must vanish on: an open set containing the whole patch image, not merely the boundary curve, and point to the companion page's witness for a closed field on a domain that carries no such patch.

items.title: The normal component of the curl is the limiting circulation per unit area of shrinking discs
items.strategy: Given a unit vector $n$, choose unit $a,b$ orthogonal to each other with $a\times b=n$: an orthonormal basis extension gives an orthonormal pair spanning the orthogonal complement, whose cross product is a unit vector orthogonal to both, hence $\pm n$, and replacing $b$ by $-b$ fixes the sign. Parametrize the disc of radius $r$ about $p$ in that plane by $\varphi(\rho,\theta)=p+\rho\cos\theta\,a+\rho\sin\theta\,b$ on a rectangle, a $C^2$ patch regular in the interior with $\varphi_\rho\times\varphi_\theta=\rho\,n$. Its induced boundary chain has the two radial edges traversed oppositely, so they cancel, and the inner edge is constant, so the circulation is the integral around the boundary circle. Stokes then turns it into $\int\langle\operatorname{curl}F(\varphi),n\rangle\rho$, and Fubini gives area $\pi r^2$. Subtract the constant value at $p$ and estimate by continuity.

items.title: Green's theorem is the curl statement for a planar field lifted to $\mathbb R^3$
items.strategy: Lift a $C^1$ planar field $(P,Q)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ to the field $(P,Q,0)$ on the open cylinder $U\times\mathbb R$, which is $C^1$ with the same partial derivatives in the first two coordinates and none in the third. Its curl has $x$ and $y$ coordinates zero and $z$ coordinate $\partial_xQ-\partial_yP$, exactly Green's integrand. The identity is therefore the published Green theorem restated, and this dictionary is what makes the planar and spatial statements one development rather than two. Verify each curl coordinate rather than only the third.

items.title: The planar divergence theorem: the flux form of Green's theorem
items.strategy: Apply Green's theorem to the rotated field $(-F_y,F_x)$: its Green integrand is $\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y$, the planar divergence. The boundary integral is $\int_{\partial D}(-F_y)\,dx+F_x\,dy$, and on an arc with nowhere vanishing derivative that integrand is the arc length integral of $\langle F,n\rangle$ with $n$ the unit vector obtained by rotating the tangent a quarter turn clockwise. State the identity in the $dx,dy$ form, which needs no regularity, and record the normal reading as a separate clause under the extra hypothesis, since the published boundary arcs may have vanishing derivative.

items.title: What the classical divergence and Stokes theorems here do and do not cover

title: The Divergence Theorem and Classical Stokes: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The closed unit box, with its six faces, is an elementary solid region
items.strategy: Parametrize each of the six faces of $[0,1]^3$ by the two free coordinates on the unit square, choosing the parameter order in each case so that the oriented area vector points out of the box; compute all six cross products explicitly. For the $z$ direction the base is the unit square with the constant graphs $0$ and $1$, the top face is the upper list, the bottom face the lower list, and the four side faces have vanishing third coordinate of the area vector. The projections of the top and bottom faces are the open unit square, whose complement in the base has content zero. The $x$ and $y$ directions are the same computation with the roles of the faces permuted, and the same six patches serve all three.

items.title: Both sides of the divergence theorem for $F(x,y,z)=(x^2,y^2,z^2)$ on the closed unit box
items.strategy: The divergence is $2(x+y+z)$, and Fubini with the fundamental theorem on the unit cube gives volume integral $3$. On the boundary, the faces $x=0$, $y=0$ and $z=0$ contribute nothing because the matching component of $F$ vanishes there, and each of the faces $x=1$, $y=1$ and $z=1$ contributes $1$. The two sides agree at $3$. Evaluate every one of the six face integrals rather than invoking symmetry.

items.title: The closed ball is an elementary solid region, presented by the eight spherical octants
items.strategy: Cut the spherical parameter rectangle into eight closed rectangles by $\phi=\pi/2$ and $\theta\in\{\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\}$ and use $\varphi(\phi,\theta)=R(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,\cos\phi)$ on each; the oriented area vector is $R\sin\phi\,\varphi$, outward, so its coordinates are $R^2\sin\phi$ times $(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,\cos\phi)$. In the $z$ direction the base is the closed disc of radius $R$ with graphs $\mp\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}$, the four octants with $\phi<\pi/2$ are the upper list and the other four the lower list, and the projections are the four open quarter discs. In the $x$ direction the split is by the sign of $\cos\theta$ and in the $y$ direction by the sign of $\sin\theta$, and in each case the vanishing set is a parameter boundary. Show that the same eight patches serve all three directions; this is the point of cutting at both $\phi=\pi/2$ and the four quadrants.

items.title: The volume of a closed ball recovered from the outward flux of the position field
items.strategy: On each octant the integrand $\langle\varphi,\varphi_\phi\times\varphi_\theta\rangle$ is $R^3\sin\phi$, so the eight patch integrals add to $4\pi R^3$. A third of that is $\tfrac43\pi R^3$, which is the published volume of the closed three-ball; state the agreement as a check of the orientation convention, since an inward presentation would give the negative.

items.title: A right circular cylinder is an elementary solid region, presented by two caps and four side quarters
items.strategy: Present the boundary of $\{x^2+y^2\le R^2,\ 0\le z\le H\}$ by two polar cap patches and four quarter side patches $\sigma(\theta,z)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z)$ on the quadrant rectangles, with outward oriented area vectors $(0,0,\pm r)$ and $R(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$ respectively. In the $z$ direction the caps are the upper and lower lists over the closed disc with constant graphs and the sides are lateral. In the $x$ direction the base is the rectangle $[-R,R]\times[0,H]$ with graphs $\mp\sqrt{R^2-y^2}$, the two side quarters with $\cos\theta>0$ are the upper list, the other two the lower list, and the caps are lateral; the projections are the two open halves of the base rectangle. The $y$ direction splits by the sign of $\sin\theta$. This is why the side is cut into four quarters rather than taken whole.

items.title: The inverse-square field is divergence free, and its flux through a sphere missing the origin vanishes
items.strategy: For $F(p)=p/\lVert p\rVert_2^3$ on $\mathbb R^3$ without the origin, differentiate each component and collect: the three terms $\lVert p\rVert^{-3}$ sum to $3\lVert p\rVert^{-3}$ and the three terms $-3p_i^2\lVert p\rVert^{-5}$ sum to $-3\lVert p\rVert^{-3}$, so the divergence is zero. Take the ball of radius $1$ about $(0,0,2)$, an elementary solid region by translating the octant presentation, with the origin outside it; the field is $C^1$ on an open set containing it, so the divergence-free corollary gives flux zero. Verify explicitly that the translated graphs are still continuous and that the translated patches are still regular.

items.title: The outward flux of the inverse-square field through a sphere centred at the origin is $4\pi$
items.strategy: Compute directly on the spherical patch of radius $R$: the oriented area vector is $R\sin\phi\,\varphi$ and the field at $\varphi$ is $\varphi/R^3$, so the integrand is $\sin\phi$ and the integral over the parameter rectangle is $4\pi$, independent of $R$. The divergence theorem is not available here and must not be invoked: the field is not defined at the origin, so it is not $C^1$ on an open set containing the ball. Say that in the item.

items.title: FALSE: a field with vanishing divergence has zero outward flux through the boundary of every solid it surrounds
items.strategy: The inverse-square field has vanishing divergence at every point where it is defined, and its outward flux through the unit sphere is $4\pi$. The false claim quietly weakens the hypothesis of the divergence-free corollary from $C^1$ on an open set containing the whole solid to $C^1$ where the field happens to be defined. Name the exact hypothesis that fails and contrast the two computations on the companion items; do not say that the divergence theorem fails, because its hypotheses were never met.

items.title: A U-shaped prism is a finite gluing of three boxes and is not simple in every coordinate direction
items.strategy: Take the union of the three boxes $[0,3]\times[0,1]\times[0,1]$, $[0,1]\times[1,3]\times[0,1]$ and $[2,3]\times[1,3]\times[0,1]$. Their interiors are disjoint and they meet in two rectangular faces. The bar's face on the plane $y=1$ is LARGER than either upright's matching face, so present that face not as one patch but as three, cut at $x=1$ and $x=2$; two of the three are then declared internal and paired with the uprights' faces by an orientation-reversing reparametrization, and the third stays outer. Subdividing a face keeps the presentation adapted in every direction, since the three projections are disjoint and fill it. Without that subdivision the pairing the gluing definition demands does not exist. For $y$ strictly between $1$ and $3$ the section in the $x$ direction is a union of two disjoint intervals, so no description of the solid as simple in the $x$ direction exists and the gluing clause is doing real work. Verify the divergence theorem on the union for the field $(x,0,0)$, where both sides are the volume $7$.

items.title: The planar divergence theorem on a rectangle, checked against a direct boundary computation
items.strategy: On $[0,1]^2$ with the field $F(x,y)=(x^2,xy)$ the planar divergence is $3x$ and the area integral is $3/2$. Traverse the four positively oriented edges, evaluate $\int(-F_y)\,dx+F_x\,dy$ on each, and add: the bottom edge contributes $0$, the right edge $1$, the top edge $1/2$ and the left edge $0$, so the four add to $3/2$. Also record the circulation form on the same field to display both readings of Green's theorem, and check that the outward unit normal on each edge is the rotation the corollary names.

items.title: A function with vanishing Laplacian has zero boundary flux of its gradient on the unit box
items.strategy: Take $v(x,y,z)=x^2-y^2$, whose Laplacian is zero, and $u$ the constant $1$ in Green's first identity: the inner-product term drops and the identity says the boundary flux of $\nabla v$ vanishes. Verify it directly on the six faces of the unit box, where the faces $x=0,1$ contribute $0$ and $2$ and the faces $y=0,1$ contribute $0$ and $-2$, and the two $z$ faces contribute nothing. State the check as a check, not as a proof of the identity.

items.title: Stokes' theorem on a flat disc and on a hemisphere with the same induced boundary circle
items.strategy: For $F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0)$ the curl is the constant $(0,0,2)$. On the flat disc parametrized in polar coordinates over a rectangle the induced boundary chain reduces to the unit circle once the two radial edges cancel and the degenerate inner edge contributes nothing, and both sides equal $2\pi$. On the upper unit hemisphere parametrized by $(\phi,\theta)$ over $[0,\pi/2]\times[0,2\pi]$ the induced boundary chain reduces to the same circle, and the curl flux is again $2\pi$. Present the shared boundary chain explicitly rather than asserting that the two surfaces span the same curve.

items.title: FALSE: Stokes' theorem requires the surface to be a graph over a coordinate plane
items.strategy: The lateral surface of a cylinder is the image of a $C^2$ patch over a rectangle and is not the graph of a function over any of the three coordinate planes: over the $xy$ plane its projection is a circle carrying a whole interval of heights, and over each of the other two it is two-valued. Verify Stokes on it for the explicit field $F(x,y,z)=(-yz,xz,0)$, whose curl is $(-x,-y,2z)$: the induced boundary chain is the bottom circle traversed with increasing azimuth together with the top circle traversed with decreasing azimuth, the two seam edges cancelling, and both sides equal $-2\pi$. Read the four edges off the published positive boundary of the parameter rectangle rather than assuming which circle is reversed. The hypothesis the theorem actually uses is that the parameter region is a finite elementary Green region, not that the image is a graph.

items.title: A curl-free $C^1$ field on the complement of a line that is not conservative
items.strategy: Take $F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0)/(x^2+y^2)$ on the complement of the $z$ axis. Differentiate to see that all three coordinates of the curl vanish. Its circulation around the unit circle in the plane $z=0$ is $2\pi$, so by the published zero-circulation property of conservative fields it has no potential. The domain is connected and open but not star-shaped, which is exactly the hypothesis of the star-shaped corollary that fails; the planar restriction of this field is the published vortex counterexample, and the item says so in prose.

items.title: The Mobius band presented by two regular patches, with the induced normals on the two overlap components
items.strategy: Use $\Psi(t,s)=((1+s\cos(t/2))\cos t,(1+s\cos(t/2))\sin t,s\sin(t/2))$ with $|s|\le 1/2$, restricted to two closed parameter rectangles in $t$ that together cover a full turn and overlap in two disjoint closed $t$ intervals. Verify that each restriction is a regular patch, compute the induced normals on the two overlap components, and show that the images agree while the normals agree on one component and are opposite on the other. Give the two normal fields explicitly at a named point of each overlap component, since the whole force of the next item is that this sign pattern is what no reorientation can repair.

items.title: FALSE: the patches of a finite presentation can always be reoriented to make their normals agree on overlaps
items.strategy: Reorienting a patch replaces its induced normal by the opposite one, so a presentation by two patches admits exactly four orientation choices, and only the relative sign of the two matters. On the Mobius presentation of the preceding item the two overlap components force opposite relative signs, so each of the four choices fails on one component. Enumerate all four rather than arguing by parity, and state the conclusion for that presentation: it is what makes the compatibility clause of a finite patch presentation a real restriction and not a normalisation.
